what_its_for: Ipilimumab is a medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including melanoma (a type of skin cancer), kidney cancer, colorectal cancer, liver cancer, lung cancer, and others. It works by helping your immune system (your body's natural defense system) recognize and fight cancer cells more effectively. It belongs to a group of medicines called 'checkpoint inhibitors' or 'immunotherapy.'
how_to_take: Ipilimumab is NOT a pill you take at home. It is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is dripped directly into your vein through a needle or port. A nurse or doctor will give you this infusion at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. Each infusion usually takes about 30 to 90 minutes. You will need to sit or lie still during the infusion. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your exact dose based on your body weight and the type of cancer being treated. Common schedules include receiving a dose every 3 weeks for 4 doses, or every 6 weeks when combined with other immunotherapy medicines. Your doctor may also adjust your dose or schedule depending on how your body responds to the medicine. Always follow the schedule your doctor and care team give you.
missed_dose: Because ipilimumab is given to you by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital, it is unlikely you will miss a dose on your own. However, if you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, contact your doctor or care team as soon as possible. Do not try to adjust or skip doses without talking to your doctor first. Your treatment schedule is carefully planned, so it is important to stick to it as closely as possible.
storage: You do not need to store ipilimumab at home, as it is prepared and given to you by healthcare professionals at the clinic. If you are ever given instructions about handling or storing this medicine, follow those directions carefully and ask your pharmacist or nurse if you have any questions.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking other medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements without telling your doctor first, as some may interfere with how ipilimumab works. Do not get any live vaccines (such as the nasal flu spray or shingles vaccine Zostavax) during treatment without asking your doctor. Tell your doctor if you are taking steroids or other medicines that suppress your immune system, as these may affect your treatment. Avoid activities that could expose you to serious infections. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 3 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Ipilimumab works by boosting your immune system, which can sometimes cause serious side effects because your immune system may accidentally attack healthy organs. Call your doctor RIGHT AWAY or go to the emergency room if you notice any of these warning signs: severe diarrhea, bloody or mucus-filled stools, severe stomach pain or cramping, yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe nausea or vomiting, unusual tiredness, shortness of breath or new cough, chest pain, irregular heartbeat, severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or changes in behavior, blurry or double vision, rash covering a large area of your body or painful blisters, muscle weakness or joint pain, decreased urine output, or swelling in your legs. Also report any signs of infusion reactions during or shortly after your IV infusion, such as chills, fever, flushing, rash, low blood pressure, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Ipilimumab does not work immediately. It may take several weeks or even months before you start to notice improvement in your cancer. Some patients may even see their tumors temporarily appear larger before they shrink, which can sometimes happen with immunotherapy. Your doctor will use scans and tests to check how well the medicine is working. Be patient and keep all of your follow-up appointments. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor, even if you feel the medicine is not working yet.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use ipilimumab if you are pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for 3 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 3 months after your last dose. Children: Ipilimumab can be used in children 6 years of age and older for certain conditions, but the dose will be carefully calculated by the doctor. Older Adults (65+): Older adults can receive this medicine, but may need to be monitored closely for side effects. Liver or Kidney Problems: Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney problems, as your doctor may need to monitor you more closely or adjust your care plan.
